data.dotgithub#.github:
Shared community health files, Renovate runner and preset for the go-fleettools organisation. Repository →
It has no tag, and no release: it is configuration, and its README is two lines long (a title and the sentence above). GitHub applies the community health files of a .github repository to the organisation’s repositories that have none of their own. There is nothing to install.

data.fleetfind#fleetfind:
Which repository already does this? A live, dated inventory of every organisation, because a hand-kept capability map drifts. Repository → Latest tag: v0.2.0; this page is written from its README at that tag. The README at that tag gives no install line; one was added on main on 2026-10-26, after checking that it builds:
go install github.com/go-fleettools/fleetfind@latest fleetfind -refresh # ~335 calls, one dated inventory fleetfind odf rtf markdown go-odf/odf ODT (OpenDocument Text) ⇄ richdoc converter, pure Go (CGO-free) go-rtf/rtf RTF <-> richdoc converter, pure Go (CGO-free) go-richdoc/markdown Markdown (CommonMark + GFM) <-> richdoc converter 3 of 2023 repositories, inventory of 2026-10-08 (The README’s example, with the date of its inventory.)
data.ranking#Ranking:
A name beats a description: a path match scores 10 and a description or topic match 3. Every term must match, so two words narrow, they do not widen.
A hit is a lead, not an authority. Confirm it:
gh api repos// --jq '{full_name, id, pushed_at, archived}'
data.rules#What it will not let you believe: Every answer carries the date the inventory was taken, and one older than a day says so on stderr before it answers: a “nothing matches” is only as good as when it was measured. Zero results are said out loud, because a sweep that prints nothing is indistinguishable from one that could not read. An empty fleet is refused, twice and separately (no organisations listed; organisations that listed and brought back no repository), and neither writes an empty inventory over a good one. Archived repositories are found but not returned by default; -all asks for them, because knowing something moved is the useful answer.

data.built-in#What is built into them: They say when they are not the code in this repository (a binary installed from an old tag is compared with what changed for that command). Every one answers -h with 0. redscan -h once ran a full sweep of every organisation, and a test now fails any command that cannot answer -h. A sweep asks for the hourly API budget before spending it and refuses to begin below a floor, because that budget is per user and shared with the fleet’s Renovate runners. A failed call must never become a verdict, and a budget stop is reported separately from “could not be read”.
data.commands#The commands:
The directories under cmd/ at v0.40.0 are:
abbench blobpurge brandcheck brief buildscan buildtag clonescan covblocks cronscan docscan docscheck docsversions docsym glmerge gopin gorequires gvlscan hostload i18ncheck judgescan landingmigrate langcheck mantracheck mkdocs2hextra modrename pagescheck pagespublish pagesretire pagetext pinscan pngeq prmerge prscan qemufix quietscan redscan relverify sitelinks tagcells tagscan testscan treecmp truncspill unarc vscan vulngate vulnscan wasmsize wfaudit The README’s table, which opens with the sweeps written on 2026-08-30, describes some of them, for example:
Command What it does redscan every default branch whose last run failed. A red branch is not a broken one: check when it last ran prscan open pull requests across every organisation, batching organisations so that about 20 search calls replace 320 prmerge merges dependency pull requests that are mergeable and fully green tagscan every tagged Go module whose default branch is ahead of its latest tag, work that is merged and that go get cannot reach. It asks about tags, not releases The organisation’s profile README (the organisation’s own index of the commands, which it says “nothing else can find”) groups thirty of the 49 by the question they answer. It predates part of cmd/ (49 directories at v0.40.0, each with a main.go, counted on 2026-10-26), so the list is not complete:
Is the fleet green? redscan, quietscan (organisations whose Renovate runner stopped: a runner that stops does not fail, it says nothing), prscan, prmerge, relverify (whether a tagged release is what its tag says). Is what is merged reachable, and is the version right? tagscan, vscan, tagcells, gorequires. Does the CI actually test it? testscan, judgescan (tests that look for an external tool the CI never installs), covblocks, buildscan, buildtag. Is it safe? vulnscan (which repositories reach a known vulnerability), vulngate (the per-repository half), wfaudit, blobpurge. Is it advertised, and is the page what it builds? docscan (every repository an organisation has and does not advertise), pagescheck, docsym, i18ncheck. What does it cost, and on what? wasmsize, hostload, truncspill, gvlscan, gopin. The small ones: brief (runs a command, shows the end of what it said, and keeps its exit status), unarc, modrename. pagespublish publishes a documentation version in the workflows of every docs site, this one included.
data.fleettools#fleettools:
Sweeps across about 1800 repositories and about 320 organisations: which default branches are red, which runners stopped, which modules are ahead of their tag, which foreign judges the CI never installs, and which tests exist without ever running. Repository → Latest tag: v0.40.0; this page is written from the top of its README at that tag, which is long (about 430 lines), and from the layout of the repository. Read the README for each command.
The sweeps were written to get every default branch green, and the README says why each one is built the way it is. It has one directory per sweep under cmd/; the module is github.com/go-fleettools/fleettools, and a command is installed as Go installs tools (the README’s example is go install .../cmd/vulngate@v0.18.1).
data.quietscan#quietscan: The README devotes sections to quietscan, the sweep for stopped Renovate runners: “What quietscan is, and the five rules it will not soften”, attribution (“the property belongs to whatever COVERS the repository”), “A failed call must never become a verdict”, “What one pass costs, and when not to run it”, and “Two things quietscan is not”. Read them there before scheduling it beside another sweep.

data.fuzzrun#fuzzrun:
Run every Go fuzz target of a module, in parallel within a load budget, and report crashers. Repository → Latest tag: v0.1.0; this page is written from its README at that tag.
go test -fuzz runs one target of one package at a time, so a module with thirty targets needs thirty commands, and a run left unattended either overloads the machine or leaves it idle. fuzzrun finds the targets, runs a few at once, waits for the machine to be quiet enough before starting each one, keeps one log per target, and says in a summary which target crashed and where the corpus file that reproduces it was written.
data.run#fuzzrun run: fuzzrun run [--dir .] [--time 10m] [--jobs 3] [--parallel 2] \ [--max-load 0] [--logs DIR] [--package pattern...] Targets are found by parsing the *_test.go files (go/parser, not a regular expression): top-level func FuzzXxx(f *testing.F). .git and testdata are skipped, and a test file that does not parse is an error, never silently zero targets. Each target runs as go test -run=^$ -fuzz=^Name$ -fuzztime=D -parallel=P ./pkg with GOWORK=off, at most --jobs at a time, its output in /-.log. --max-load L (L > 0): before starting each target, wait while the 1-minute load average is above L. It is read from sysctl vm.loadavg on darwin and /proc/loadavg on linux. Where it cannot be read, run exits 2 up front instead of pretending the machine was quiet. --package keeps only matching packages (repeatable). A target that fails with a Failing input written to testdata/fuzz// line is a CRASH, and the summary gives that path relative to the module. Any other failing exit is a FAIL, with the log to read. PASS ./. FuzzGood 5s CRASH ./. FuzzBad 1.2s testdata/fuzz/FuzzBad/6f1c... 2 targets: 1 PASS, 0 FAIL, 1 CRASH Exit status: 0 every target passed, 1 at least one FAIL or CRASH, 2 the run could not be made (no go.mod, no targets, go missing, bad flags, unreadable load with --max-load).
data.wait#fuzzrun wait: fuzzrun wait FILE SUBSTRING [--timeout 10m] [--interval 2s] Blocks until FILE contains SUBSTRING, for example a log written by a background fuzzrun run. It prints found (exit 0) or timeout (exit 1); exit 2 on a read error other than the file not existing yet.
data.why#Why: The fuzz targets of a module are a security control only if they are actually run, all of them, for long enough, without taking the machine down. The tool came out of the go-llmflow/gateway security audit, where thirty targets were run by hand with a shell loop that could not tell a crash from a timeout. Its tests plant a failing target and require run to report it with its corpus path and exit 1; the module is copied to a temporary directory first, so the corpus a crash writes never lands in the repository.

data.landingdiff#landingdiff:
Which of a set of landing pages is the odd one out, by counting what each page puts in the shared design system. Repository → Latest tag: v0.2.0; this page is written from its README at that tag. The README at that tag gives no install line; one was added on main on 2026-10-26, after checking that it builds:
go install github.com/go-fleettools/landingdiff@latest landingdiff ../landing-go-*/layouts/index.html go-authn go-fileshare go-pkgx go-pdfkit spread headline line 1, characters 14 10 19 23 10..23 items in the trust band 3 3 3 4 3..4 <- go-pdfkit buttons in the hero 2 2 2 2 ... go-pdfkit is alone on 2 measure(s) (An excerpt of the README’s example.)
data.limits#What it will not tell you: A page is named only when the others agree and it does not: one value held by everybody else, one page holding something different. It deliberately does not flag “furthest from the rest”, which would name the smallest and the largest every time. It is blind to layout. A headline too long for its column is a fact about rendering, found by screenshotting the pages; use both, because neither finds the other’s. Read the comment on the line before you “fix” an outlier: an outlier the history explains is not drift. To add a measure, add one entry in measures: a name and a function from the page’s HTML to a count, returning -1, not 0, when the part is not there at all.
data.why#Why counting, and not diffing: The landings share one styles.html, so “aligned” cannot be checked by diffing the design system. What drifts is what each page puts in it: a band with one more item than fits on a line, a navigation with twice as many links as its neighbours.

data.brand#landingkit brand: landingkit brand static/img/logo.svg >> hugo.toml # then remove the old block The brand colour is read from the logo’s gradient, never chosen, and it is the only thing an organisation sets: the first two stop-color of the SVG give a dark stop (base, which carries text on white) and a light one (bright, the accent in dark mode), and every other value is derived. The block also records both contrast ratios, so a logo too light to carry text is visible in the diff that introduces it. Backgrounds, surfaces and greys belong to the sheet and cannot be configured.
data.import#Importing it: # hugo.toml [module] [[module.imports]] path = "github.com/go-fleettools/landingkit" # go.mod, at the root of the site: Hugo resolves modules with the go command module github.com//.github.io go 1.27.3 require github.com/go-fleettools/landingkit v0.12.0 Add a kit.go next to it, behind a tools build tag, importing the module: without it go mod tidy finds nothing that uses the module and deletes the requirement. The Pages workflow needs actions/setup-go before hugo. A site’s own layouts/partials/ still wins over the module’s. The README has the exact steps.
data.landingkit#landingkit:
The go-* landing pages’ shared design, as a Hugo module, and the command that derives a landing’s brand from its logo and checks a landing against the reference. Repository → Latest tag: v0.12.0; this page is written from its README at that tag. The landing of this very organisation uses it.
Before the kit, every landing copied the partials and the copies drifted. A landing that imports the module cannot drift; it can only fall behind a version, and Renovate proposes the bump.
data.links#landingkit links: landingkit links [-attempts 3] [-wait 3s] [-timeout 25s] public Every http(s) URL in the built site must answer 2xx or 3xx, with redirects followed, each URL tried three times. A github.com blob link is checked on the raw host, since github.com answers a program with 503 most of the time. workflows/links.yml is a template for a landing’s link check.
data.parts#What is in the module: The partials include the whole design (styles.html, brand colours from [params.brand]), the theme toggle (system, light, dark), the fork ribbon, the Octicons icons, a loading carousel, a hero carousel, the mantra strip, an opt-in red btn-try button, and a language selector with the words the partials write in seven languages. The README documents each, with the version that added it.

data.install#Install and usage:
GOBIN=~/.local/bin go install github.com/go-fleettools/modfloor@latest modfloor --dir ~/Documents/VCS/GIT/localhost --owners 'go-*' --floor 1.27.3 modfloor --bins ~/.local/bin --floor 1.27.3 modfloor --floor 1.27.3 github.com/go-fleettools/fleettools Verdicts, kept apart because they call for different work:
Verdict Meaning ok the go directive is at or above the floor toolchain the directive is below it, but a toolchain line pins higher: the build fails closed under GOTOOLCHAIN=local. Not an exposure BELOW the directive is below the floor and nothing pins higher: the exposure no-go no go directive at all unreadable a directive that is not a Go version Exit status: 0 clean, 1 at least one module exposed, 2 the measurement could not be made.
data.modfloor#modfloor:
The Go toolchain floor a module declares, against the floor a fix requires. Repository → Latest tag: v0.2.0; this page is written from its README at that tag.
A repository can be green, released and built with a patched toolchain while still shipping a vulnerable floor to everyone downstream. Three pins decide three different things: go-version: in a workflow builds the artefacts; the toolchain recorded in a binary says what one installed executable was built with; and the go directive in the published go.mod is what a consumer honours under GOTOOLCHAIN=local. Only the third is the exposure, and no green check looks at it.
data.reads#What it reads, and what it refuses:
It reads the published go.mod from proxy.golang.org, where a consumer reads it too, not the working tree (which may hold an unreleased fix) and not a workflow. It spends no GitHub API budget and needs no credential. --owners is a declared population, and every number in the report is about that set; a module in no git work tree, or under another owner, is set aside and counted. A measurement that found nothing refuses rather than reporting a clean fleet.
Two traps it encodes: go/version accepts go27.2 (a typo that compares above every real version), so the floor is validated; and modfile.ParseLax does not fill File.Toolchain, so the directive is recovered from the syntax tree.
The README names its siblings: vulnscan and vulngate for the advisories themselves, gopin for the CI pin, and staletools for installed binaries.

data.excluded#A file the build excludes:
A //go:build js && wasm file is not in a native build, so deleting a refusal in it changes nothing the command can see: the verdict would be SURVIVED when nothing looked. mutsweep reads GOOS and GOARCH as the go tool does. Naming an excluded file in -files or -only is an error (exit 2), and a directory sweep skips such files and names them.
The README also describes -tally, for planning and auditing a campaign swept in chunks; read it there.
data.install#Install: go install github.com/go-fleettools/mutate@latest # one mutation go install github.com/go-fleettools/mutate/mutsweep@latest # every refusal in a package
data.mutate#mutate:
Prove that a test can fail. Apply one exact source mutation, run the suite, restore whatever happens, and exit 0 only when the suite went red. Repository → Latest tag: v0.7.0; this page is written from its README at that tag. It has no dependency beyond the standard library.
$ mutate -file browse.go -name "mark repeats too" \ -from 'if !n.Repeat {' -to 'if true {' \ -- go test -run TestARepeatIsNot ./... mutate: mark repeats too — caught
data.mutsweep#mutsweep: the same question, of:
mutate proves one test can fail. mutsweep asks it of every refusal in a package: it deletes each one in turn, and says which ones nothing noticed.
$ mutsweep -dir structured -files blob.go,cell.go -run-in . -- go test ./... mutsweep: 38 refusals, 3m0s each at most, through "go test ./..." [1/38] caught blob.go:366 (size == 0) != (count == 0) 5s [15/38] SURVIVED blob.go:347 used <= 0 12s ... 38 refusals: 15 caught, 21 not mutants, 2 survived, 0 hung what nothing holds: SURVIVED blob.go:347 used <= 0 SURVIVED cell.go:98 !ok The README reports that over five runs on one project it put 574 guards through this and found thirteen that no test held.
data.only#Answering a report: -only:
After a sweep, tests are written for the survivors, and the question becomes whether they kill them, which is not the same as whether they pass. -only re-asks it for the named targets, spelled as the report prints them:
mutsweep -only map.go:163,map.go:628 -timeout 2m -- go test -count 1 ./... A target that matches no refusal is an error naming it, because an -only list goes stale and a sweep of nothing reads like a clean one.

data.install#Install: go install github.com/go-fleettools/prwait@latest It shells out to gh, which holds the authentication: prwait never reads, prints or passes a token.
data.prwait#prwait:
Wait until a pull request’s checks are finished, and refuse to call an empty check list a pass. Repository → Latest tag: v0.5.0; this page is written from its README at that tag.
$ prwait -repo go-pkgx/pkgx 82 83 go-pkgx/pkgx#82 PASS SUCCESS:24 go-pkgx/pkgx#83 FAIL test (windows-latest)=FAILURE $ prwait go-pkgx/bk#311 go-pkgx/mirror#28 go-pkgx/bk#311 FAIL CONFLICTING — rebase it; any green ticks it shows are from the old base go-pkgx/mirror#28 PASS SUCCESS:20 SKIPPED:1 Exit Meaning 0 every pull request finished, with checks, and all of them acceptable 1 one finished red, conflicts, was closed, or ran out of time 2 refused: bad usage, or an answer that could not be read
data.rule#The rule:
A pull request passes only when at least -min-checks checks exist, every one of them has finished, and every conclusion is acceptable. Absence is never evidence.
An obvious waiter asks “is anything still pending?” and stops when the answer is no; that waiter reported success on four pull requests that had never been built. A conflicted pull request gets no merge ref, so no workflow runs and its check list stays empty, and the same list is empty right after a push and for the life of a pull request whose workflow fails to parse. Also: a commit status is not a check run; CANCELLED is not a pass (NEUTRAL and SKIPPED are); UNKNOWN mergeability is not an answer; a timeout is a failure; an error from gh sinks the run.
data.usage#Usage: prwait [-repo OWNER/REPO] [flags] ... Target Asks 82 or OWNER/REPO#82 a pull request: may this land @main or OWNER/REPO@main a branch: is what landed green !40237685388 or OWNER/REPO!402... a workflow run: did that dispatch finish, and how Flag Default -repo repository for bare numbers -interval 45s how often to ask -timeout 30m give up after this, per run -min-checks 1 how many checks must exist before a pass is possible -gh gh the gh binary to ask -min-checks 0 is refused, because it would restore the defect this tool exists for. The number is one for the whole run, so split the run when suites differ.

data.install#Install and usage: go install github.com/go-fleettools/staletools@latest staletools [-all] [-want go1.27.1] [dir...] With no directory it looks at $GOBIN (or $GOPATH/bin, or ~/go/bin) and ~/.local/bin. -want compares against another toolchain: “what would be stale if we moved to this?”. It has no dependency beyond the standard library.
data.releases#-releases: staletools -releases The default axis asks what a tool was built with; this one asks what it is: which installed tools are an older release of themselves. A marker → flags those in a directory the shell searches, ahead of those in one nothing reads. The oracle is go list -m -versions, not a tag listing, and a tool built from an unreleased commit is reported under its own heading rather than mislabelled as behind.
data.staletools#staletools:
Which installed Go tools were built with an older toolchain, and, of those, which actually parse Go source, because only for those is staleness a wrong answer rather than an old binary. Repository → Latest tag: v0.3.0; this page is written from its README at that tag.
$ staletools READ GO SOURCE and are behind go1.27.1 — these do not fail, they MISREPORT: gopls go1.26.4 ~/go/bin go install golang.org/x/tools/gopls@latest ... INSTALLED TWICE with different toolchains — PATH order decides which runs: agentsync go1.27.1 ~/.local/bin go1.26.4 ~/go/bin 81 Go tool(s), 29 behind go1.27.1, 8 of those read Go source (An excerpt of the README’s example, measured on its author’s machine.)
Exit 0 no source-reading tool is behind, and nothing is shadowed 1 something is behind or shadowed 2 refused: a directory that cannot be read
data.why#Why the distinction: A CLI built with go1.26 runs under a go1.27 toolchain: it is old, not broken. But a tool that analyses Go source embeds go/types and go/parser from its build toolchain, and built with go1.26 it cannot read go1.27: it emits type errors about the standard library and then reports on whatever it managed to load, so the output reads like findings. staletools finds those tools from the dependency list of the binary (golang.org/x/tools, honnef.co/go/tools and the like), not from a list of names. It also reports a tool installed in two directories with different toolchains. The totals are always printed, zeros included.

data.lead#A lead, not a verdict:
Both shapes are correct over input the program produced itself, so every hit has to be read by somebody who knows where the bytes come from. What the tool owes in return: it parses rather than greps; it names what it could not read; it prints both denominators (“66 repositories read, 0 NOT read”); and reading nothing is a failure, exiting non-zero.
A directory is scanned in place so that the instrument can be checked against a checkout of a version that had the defect: it must find it, and find nothing on the fixed version.
data.limits#What it does not cover: The image decoders are a written-out list, so a third-party HEIC or JPEG 2000 reader is a decoder it does not know. A ZIP entry read through a helper in another file is missed: the two shapes are judged within one file. It holds 100 % statement coverage, gated in CI.
data.unbounded#unbounded:
Which repositories read a ZIP entry, or decode an image, without a ceiling? Repository → Latest tag: v0.2.0; this page is written from its README at that tag. The README at that tag gives no install line; one was added on main on 2026-10-26, after checking that it builds (the command is in cmd/unbounded, the module root is not a main package):
go install github.com/go-fleettools/unbounded/cmd/unbounded@latest unbounded go-odf go-pdfkit go-gfx # organisations: listed, cloned, parsed unbounded ./some/checkout # a directory is scanned in place go-gfx/gfx svg/svg.go:817 image.Decode and nothing in this file asks DecodeConfig first go-pdfkit/pdfkit image.go:99 png.Decode and nothing in this file asks DecodeConfig first 66 repositories read, 0 NOT read 2 open a ZIP, 15 decode an image, 4 lead(s) to look at (The README’s example output.)
data.why#Why: Both shapes are how a few hundred bytes of input become a few gigabytes of memory: io.ReadAll on a ZIP entry (an .ods of 67,206 bytes inflated to 64 MiB and held 222.9 MiB), and image.Decode before image.DecodeConfig (a 75-byte PNG claiming 10000 x 10000 allocated 381.6 MiB). A fix does not travel: a sibling repository carried the identical defect for weeks because nobody looked, and this is the sweep that follows a fix across its siblings.
